title: The Twelve Steps
wordingNote: The steps are quoted from the 1939 first edition. The wording differs in places from later editions — step twelve here reads 'spiritual experience' where later editions read 'spiritual awakening'.
authorNote: Explanations and questions are written for this app. They are not official A.A. material, not from the 1952 book Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions, and are meant to be edited. Only the quoted step text and the linked passages come from the book.

explanation: Step one asks for two admissions, not one, and they are about different things. Powerless over alcohol is about what happens once you start drinking. That our lives had become unmanageable is about how things were going the rest of the time — whether or not there was a drink in your hand.

The book is blunt about the first. It says the delusion that we are like other people has to be smashed. Not managed, not worked around. Smashed. The chapter that carries most of this argument is More About Alcoholism, and it is worth reading before you write anything here.

Nothing in this step asks you to feel differently, or to have hope yet — hope is step two's business. The word the book uses is concede: to fully concede to your innermost self. That is a quieter thing than surrender, and a harder one to fake.
People come back to step one for years, usually to the second half of it. The first half tends to settle. The unmanageable part keeps finding new evidence.

questions.text: What happens to you once you take the first drink? Not what you intend to happen — what actually happens, going on the evidence.
List the ways you have tried to control it: rules, switches, breaks, geography. What did each one prove?
The book says the delusion that we are like other people has to be smashed. Where do you still quietly believe you are like other people?
Set drinking aside entirely. Where was your life unmanageable — money, work, health, promises, the people who live with you?
Who has been carrying something for you that you should have been carrying yourself?
What is the thing you would least like written down here? What makes it hard to write?
The word the book uses is concede, not admit. Is there a difference for you, and which one have you actually done?
If you are coming back to this step rather than taking it for the first time, what has changed since last time — and what has not?

work.intro: Evidence, not conclusions. Add to these over time rather than filling them in once — the second half in particular tends to keep producing examples.

explanation: Two words carry this one: came, and believe. Came, because it is arrived at rather than possessed — usually slowly, and usually after step one has left you without anywhere else to put the weight.

The book is unusually accommodating here, and people are often surprised by that. It says your own conception, however inadequate, is enough to start with, and then reduces the whole step to a single question: do you now believe, or are you even willing to believe. Willing counts. That is deliberate.

Restore us to sanity is the harder half, because of what it implies. The book means something specific and narrow by it — the moment of picking up the first drink again with every reason not to, and no memory of why not. Chapter three calls that plain insanity and means it plainly.
Nothing here asks you to settle what you believe, or to believe anything in particular. It asks you to stop insisting you already know.

questions.text: What did you actually believe before any of this? Not what you were taught, and not what you would say out loud — what you actually believed.
"Do I now believe, or am I even willing to believe." Where are you in that sentence today?
What are you unwilling to believe, and what would it cost you to turn out to be wrong about it?
The book says your own conception, however inadequate, is enough. What is yours today, in your own words rather than borrowed ones?
What has kept you sober so far that was not your own will — people, a room, a phone call, luck? Whatever you want to call it, name it.
Chapter three calls picking up the first drink again plain insanity. Where does that describe you, and where do you still argue with it?
If you are stuck on the word God, what exactly is the objection — the word, the idea behind it, or the people you associate with it?
What would have to happen for you to say you had come to believe? Would you notice if it already had?

explanation: Step three is a decision, not an achievement. The wording is careful about this: made a decision to turn our will and our lives over. The turning over is what the remaining nine steps are for. This is the decision to start.

The argument the book makes is about self-will, and it is not flattering. It describes a man trying to run the whole show — arranging the lights, the scenery and everyone else's part — convinced that things would go well if the rest of the cast would only do as he wished. It is meant to be recognisable, and for most people it is.
Then it puts the turn in eleven words: first of all, we had to quit playing God. It didn't work.

There is a prayer in the text, and many people say it with someone else in the room. It is also a decision people take more than once — after a bad week, or years later on a different question entirely — which is why this page keeps a date each time rather than one date forever.

questions.text: What are you actually deciding? Put it in your own words, without any of the borrowed language.
Where in the last month were you arranging the lights and the scenery — running a show that was not yours to run?
Whose life have you been managing besides your own, and how well has that gone for them?
"Any life run on self-will could hardly be a success." Where has your self-will actually worked? Be fair to it before you hand it over.
What are you afraid of losing if you turn this over?
What is the part you are quietly keeping back? There usually is one.
If you have taken this step before: what did the decision change, and what did it not touch at all?
Who did you take this step with, or who would you want beside you when you do?

work.intro: A decision taken more than once. Each time is kept with its date rather than replacing the last.

explanation: Step four is written down. That is not a stylistic preference — the book says it four separate times: we set them on paper, we placed them before us in black and white, we put them on paper, we got this all down on paper and looked at it. Something you have only turned over in your head is not an inventory. The image the book reaches for is a shop taking stock, a fact-finding and a fact-facing process, and it is honest about the object of the exercise: to find the damaged goods and get rid of them promptly and without regret.

Resentment comes first, and the book does not treat it as a matter of manners. It calls resentment the number one offender, says it destroys more alcoholics than anything else, and then goes considerably further than most people expect — we found that it is fatal. Not unhelpful. Fatal. The argument is that staying angry shuts you off from the one thing keeping you sober, and the drinking then takes care of the rest.

Then it turns the list round, and this is what makes it a moral inventory instead of a list of grievances. Putting out of our minds the wrongs others had done, we resolutely looked for our own mistakes. Where had we been selfish, dishonest, self-seeking and frightened? Keep the book's own line to hand for when this gets uncomfortable: the inventory was ours, not the other man's.

Two more passes follow by the same method. Fear gets a page of its own, even where no resentment attaches to it — an evil and corroding thread, the book calls it, with the fabric of our existence shot through. Then conduct, sex included and not only sex, tested by one question rather than anyone's rules: where were we at fault, and what should we have done instead. This is the step people stall on longest. It asks for thoroughness. It does not ask you to be finished by Sunday.

questions.text: What are you afraid this will turn up? Begin there — it is usually the reason the step exists.
The book asks for searching and fearless. Which of those two is harder for you, and where is it going to show?
Who would you most like to leave off the list, and what reason are you giving yourself?
When you think about a resentment, whose conduct do you find yourself explaining first — theirs, or your own?
Take one where you were genuinely, unarguably wronged. What was your part anyway?
Where has fear been running something you have been calling by a better name — caution, standards, principle, loyalty?
Whom have you hurt and never accounted for, because nobody ever made you?
What would make you stop halfway through this? Name it now, so you recognise it when it arrives.

work.intro: Three passes, in the order the book takes them. Do them one at a time. None of them is finished on the day you start, and the first is much the longest.

explanation: Step five is step four said out loud to somebody. Three hearers are named — God, yourself, and one other human being — and it is the third that people balk at. Worth knowing as you read: the step as printed says the exact nature of our wrongs, while the chapter that takes it up again says defects. It is one of the places where the 1939 text does not quite agree with itself. The work is the same either way.

The book puts its reason first and does not dress it up: if we skip this vital step, we may not overcome drinking. Then it says what it has watched happen. People took inventory all right, and hung on to some of the worst items in stock — and almost invariably got drunk, and wondered why, having done everything else. A solitary self-appraisal, it says, is not enough. You can be honest on paper in a way that costs you nothing.

On who hears it, the book is practical rather than pious. Think well before choosing. It suggests a priest if you have one, a doctor, a psychologist, or simply a close-mouthed and understanding friend — someone who can keep a confidence, who grasps what you are doing, and who will not try to change your plan. It also draws a line most people need drawing: you may not unburden yourself onto someone the telling would hurt. We have no right to save our own skin at another person's expense. Be hard on yourself, considerate of others. And if there is genuinely no one, the step may wait — but only if you are ready to take it at the first opportunity, and not as an excuse.

The account of afterwards is not modest. We can look the world in the eye. Our fears fall from us. All of it hangs on two words in the same sentence: withholding nothing. Then the book sends you home to sit somewhere quiet for an hour and read the first five steps back, asking whether the work is solid, whether the stones are properly in place, whether you tried to make mortar without sand. Be honest about what you left out. The thing you are planning not to mention is usually the thing the step is for.

questions.text: Who are you going to tell? If no name has come to mind, what is the objection to each of the ones that did?
The book wants someone who can keep a confidence and will not try to change your plan. Does the person you have in mind pass both tests?
What are you planning to leave out? Write it down here, even if you write it nowhere else.
What do you expect them to think of you afterwards? Where did that expectation come from?
Is anything in your inventory genuinely not yours to disclose — and are you certain that is the real reason for leaving it out?
The book describes people who kept back the worst items in stock and drank over it. What would yours be?
If you are postponing this: is it that there is nobody, or that there is nobody you want?
Afterwards — what actually happened, and what is still unsaid?

explanation: Sixty-five words. That is the whole of what this book gives step six, and it is worth knowing before you go looking for more. It asks one question, then asks it again harder: are we now ready to let God remove from us all the things which we have admitted are objectionable? Can He now take them all — every one?

The words doing the work are entirely and all these. Not the ones you have grown tired of, or the ones that have started to embarrass you in front of people. Then comes the sentence that looks like a way out and is not: should we still cling to something we will not let go, we ask God to help us be willing. You are not required to arrive willing. You are required to name the thing you are still holding, and stop calling it something else.

These defects points backwards, not outwards. It means the particular things on the list you made in step four — not a general audit of human failings, which is always more comfortable. If you want the book's own name for what sits underneath them, it is a chapter earlier, and it is not flattering: selfishness, self-centeredness, driven by a hundred forms of fear, self-delusion, self-seeking and self-pity.

questions.text: Go back to your step four. Which defect on it are you genuinely ready to be rid of?
Which one are you still holding? Name it plainly, without the reason attached.
What does that one still do for you? Nobody keeps a defect that has stopped paying.
The step says entirely ready, and all these. Where are you quietly negotiating for an exception?
Who would notice first if this were actually removed — and how would you feel about them noticing?
Are you willing to be made willing? That is a different question from the one above, and the book allows it.
What are you afraid you would be without it?
If you have been here before: what were you not ready for last time, and where does it stand now?

explanation: Sixty-nine words, and most of them are the prayer itself. The book does not explain step seven. It tells you what to say, and then says: we have then completed step seven. That is the entire treatment, and the brevity is not an oversight — steps six and seven are the hinge between the inventory behind you and the amends in front, and the book clearly expects you to spend less time here than you will spend on either side.

The word to sit with is humbly. Bill's own account of this working puts it about as plainly as it can be put: there had been a humble willingness to have Him with me — and He came. Not a performance of humility, and not self-abasement, which is only pride facing the other way. Something closer to the end of arguing.

One caution, which is in the book and is better had now than later. Writing to families about what to expect, it says a man's defects of character are not going to disappear over night, and that he has entered upon a period of growth. Nothing in step seven promises the shortcomings are gone by Thursday. It is asked once, and then by most people many times.

explanation: You have already made most of this list. The book says so plainly — we have a list of all persons we have harmed and to whom we are willing to make amends; we made it when we took inventory. Step eight is largely a matter of going back to step four, pulling the names out of it, and being honest about the ones you left off.

The step has two halves and only the first is clerical. Made a list is work you can do in an evening. Became willing to make amends to them all is not, and the book knows it: if we haven't the will to do this, we ask until it comes. That is the whole instruction. Not force it, not fake it, not wait for it to arrive on its own. Ask until it comes, and in the meantime keep the name on the list.

The hard part is what counts as harm. If you only write down money owed and promises broken, the list will be too short and you will know it. The book's picture is a tornado roaring through the lives of others — hearts broken, sweet relationships dead, affections uprooted — and its joke about the farmer coming up from the cyclone cellar to say don't see anything the matter here, Ma, ain't it grand the wind stopped blowin'. Sobriety is not the repair. It is what makes the repair possible.

Note what the step does not ask. Not that you forgive anyone, not that you decide who deserves an amend, not that you work out yet what you will actually do or say. Whether an amend can be made at all, and whether making it would injure someone, is step nine's problem. Here you are only naming people and telling the truth about your willingness.

explanation: Direct is the word that makes this step difficult, and it is chosen. Not an apology thought about, not a private resolution to do better, not a donation made in someone's general direction. You go to the person. The book's instruction on manner is one of the most quoted lines it has, and it is worth having by heart before you knock on anyone's door: we are there to sweep off our side of the street. His faults are not discussed. We stick to our own.

Then the exception, which is in the step itself and is not a loophole for your comfort. Except when to do so would injure them or others. The book is unusually firm here in both directions. It says do not be the hasty and foolish martyr who would needlessly sacrifice others to save himself, and it says that where other people would be implicated you secure their consent first. What it will not let you do is use somebody else's welfare as cover for your own embarrassment. The test is whether the injury would fall on them or on you.

On what it costs: you may lose your position or reputation, or face jail, and the book's answer is that you must be willing. Its promise about how these go is more modest than people remember — in nine cases out of ten the unexpected happens, feuds of years' standing can melt away in an hour, and if somebody throws you out of his office, you have still done your part. It's water over the dam. The outcome was never the thing you were responsible for.

Some of it cannot be done. There may be wrongs you can never fully right, people who cannot be seen, cases where postponement is genuinely valid rather than convenient. The book allows all three and then closes the exits: we don't worry about them if we can honestly say we would right them if we could, some people get an honest letter instead, and we don't delay if it can be avoided. Sensible, tactful, considerate, humble — and, it adds, without being servile. As God's people we stand on our feet; we don't crawl before anyone.

explanation: Something changes here, and it changes for the rest of the book. Steps one to nine are taken. Ten, eleven and twelve are practised. The book says so in as many words: this is not an overnight matter, it should continue for our life time. There is no version of step ten you complete.

It gives you four things to watch — selfishness, dishonesty, resentment and fear — which are the same four the inventory turned up, now in the present tense. And it gives you a sequence to run when one shows up, in which the striking thing is the speed. Ask at once. Discuss it immediately. Make amends quickly. Nothing here is scheduled for the weekend, because the point is to stop the thing accumulating into another step four.

Then the part people leave off when they quote it: and then we resolutely turn our thoughts to someone we can help. The inventory is not meant to end with you looking at yourself. It ends with you looking away. Love and tolerance of others is our code — which the book offers as a working method rather than as sentiment.

One caution, and it is the book's own. It is easy to let up on the spiritual program of action and rest on our laurels. What you have is described as a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition — not a cure, and not a thing you did once in a good year. If you want the reward stated, it is a page earlier: we have ceased fighting anything or anyone, even alcohol.

explanation: The step contains its own limit, and it is the most distinctive thing about it: praying only for knowledge of His will for us and the power to carry that out. Not for outcomes. Not for the thing you want, however reasonable it is. The book is not squeamish about why — left to ourselves we pray for what suits us, and then call the answer guidance.

What it actually gives you is a routine, in three parts. At night, a review: were we resentful, selfish, dishonest, or afraid? Do we owe an apology? Were we thinking of ourselves most of the time? On waking, a request that the day's thinking be directed, and specifically that it be divorced from self-pity, dishonest or self-seeking motives. And through the day, a pause — we pause when agitated or doubtful and ask for the right thought or action.

That nightly review sits under step eleven in this book, although it reads like step ten and most people work it there. Both readings are defensible. It is worth knowing that the arrangement is the book's, not a mistake in this app.

The book is also practical about the parts that do not come easily. On indecision: we ask for an intuitive thought, then we relax and take it easy, we don't struggle — and it admits that early on you are unlikely to be much good at telling inspiration from your own preferences. On self-consciousness about prayer: we shouldn't be shy on this matter, better men than we are using it constantly. And on the whole apparatus, four words that are either the most honest or the most infuriating in the chapter, depending on the day: it works — it really does.

explanation: Three clauses, and the first is a claim about you rather than an instruction. Having had a spiritual experience as the result of these steps — the 1939 wording, where later editions read awakening. The book means it as the result of the nine steps behind you, not as a separate event you wait for.

The middle clause has a whole chapter to itself, and it opens by putting the case for it entirely in terms of your own survival: nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics. It works when other activities fail. Helping others is the foundation stone of your recovery. This is not framed as charity, and the book is blunt that it costs — sleep, evenings, your business, your telephone at any hour.

It is equally blunt about restraint, which is the part that gets forgotten. Do not chase someone who will not work with you; to spend too much time on any one situation is to deny some other alcoholic an opportunity. Do not force yourself on anyone. And if he prefers a different approach entirely, encourage him to follow his own conscience — we have no monopoly on God; we merely have an approach that worked with us.

The third clause, in all our affairs, is the one that outlasts the rest. The book's test of it is not piety but ordinary competence: assuming we are spiritually fit, we can do all sorts of things alcoholics are not supposed to do. Which leaves the last page, and the only instruction the book ends on — abandon yourself to God as you understand God, clear away the wreckage of your past, give freely of what you find, and join us.
